content.text: The Eurasian lynx disappeared from Britain more than a thousand years ago, mainly because of hunting and the loss of forests. Today, some conservation groups are campaigning to bring it back to remote parts of Scotland and northern England.

Supporters argue that the lynx would help control the growing population of roe deer, which damage young trees and prevent forests from regenerating. They point to Switzerland, where lynx were reintroduced in the 1970s and now live alongside farmers with relatively few conflicts.

Sheep farmers, however, are far from convinced. They fear that lynx would attack lambs, and many feel that decisions are being made by city-based campaigners who will not have to deal with the consequences. Compensation schemes, they say, rarely cover the full cost of lost animals.

Scientists themselves are divided. Some studies suggest that lynx prefer woodland prey and rarely approach farms; others note that conditions in Britain, where forests are small and fragmented, may push lynx into closer contact with livestock.
What seems clear is that any reintroduction would need the support of local communities. Without it, the project would risk failing — not because of ecology, but because of politics.
Why did the lynx disappear from Britain? A) disease B) hunting and deforestation C) competition with deer D) climate change
Why does the writer mention Switzerland? A) to show reintroduction can work B) to criticise Swiss farmers C) to compare deer populations D) to describe lynx behaviour in mountains
What is the farmers' main concern? A) lynx would eat deer B) lynx would harm their animals C) forests would grow D) tourists would come

What does the writer suggest about the farmers' view of campaigners? A) farmers trust them B) farmers think campaigners won't suffer the effects C) campaigners live on farms D) campaigners pay compensation
What is the writer's view of compensation schemes? A) the writer doesn't give a personal view — it's the farmers' view B) they are generous C) they are unnecessary D) they always work
What does paragraph 4 show about scientists? A) they all support the project B) they disagree about the risk to livestock C) they have no data D) they oppose the project
Why might British conditions be different? A) forests are small and broken up B) there are no sheep C) deer are smaller D) winters are colder
What is the writer's main conclusion? A) the lynx should not return B) ecology is the main obstacle C) local support is essential D) Switzerland's model will fail
